stories.headline: MAY NFP +172K DOUBLES CONSENSUS — FED RATE HIKE ODDS SURGE TO 68%
stories.body: The U.S. economy added 172,000 jobs in May against a 95,000 consensus, with unemployment holding at 4.3%. CME FedWatch now prices a 68% probability of a 25 bps rate hike by December 2026, up from 52% pre-report — reversing the rate-cut narrative that opened the year.
stories.explain: The mechanism is discount rate repricing: equities are priced on discounted future cash flows, and a higher-than-expected rate path raises the 'r' in P = CF/(r − g), compressing valuations immediately. The Nasdaq 100's 3.4% decline outpaced the S&P 500's 2.5% drop because long-duration growth stocks have a greater share of their value in distant future earnings — the same earnings that get most penalized when discount rates rise. Today's selloff is not driven by bad fundamentals but by re-marking the assumed cost of capital upward by ~25 bps across all asset classes.

stories.headline: S&P 500 DROPS TO 7,330, NDX -3.4% AS RATE REPRICING EXTENDS INTO TUESDAY
stories.body: Equity markets extended Friday's post-NFP losses Tuesday, with the S&P 500 falling to 7,330 and the Nasdaq 100 shedding 3.4% to 28,419. Selling was broadest in high-multiple tech and growth names, which are most sensitive to changes in long-end yield expectations.
stories.explain: Even though the 10-year Treasury yield eased 2 basis points today to 4.54%, the terminal rate expectation — the peak rate priced into the forward curve — moved higher. This distinction matters: the spot yield fell slightly on safe-haven flows as equities sold off, but the forward rate path shifted up. Goldman Sachs acknowledged the NFP data increases the probability of a 'longer pause,' language markets are reading as hawkish. The NDX's outperformance to the downside reflects its concentration in mega-cap tech names trading at 30x+ forward earnings, where even small moves in the discount rate produce large absolute valuation changes.

stories.headline: IRAN-ISRAEL AGREE TO HALT ATTACKS; WTI FALLS $4 TO $89
stories.body: Iran and Israel agreed to halt direct attacks against each other, deflating the Middle East risk premium that had pushed WTI to $93.60 Monday. Crude fell 4.5% to $89.38 as supply disruption fears eased; President Trump indicated a Strait of Hormuz reopening deal could be reached 'soon.'
stories.explain: WTI had spiked above $93 as the Iran-Israel conflict raised genuine risk of Strait of Hormuz closure — a chokepoint handling roughly 20% of global seaborne oil. The de-escalation deflated the geopolitical risk premium embedded in the price, which functions like a volatility component layered on top of the supply-demand equilibrium price. Risk premiums unwind faster than they build: buyers who added positions on supply-disruption fears have strong incentive to exit quickly once the catalyst resolves. The remaining $89 floor reflects the underlying tight physical market; if Hormuz reopens fully, the equilibrium price likely drops closer to $82-85.

stories.headline: GOLD DROPS TO $4,276 AS SAFE-HAVEN DEMAND EVAPORATES ON IRAN CEASEFIRE
stories.body: Gold fell 1.0% to $4,276/oz as the Iran-Israel ceasefire drained geopolitical safe-haven demand, compounding pressure from the strong NFP print which elevated real rates. Gold is now down 9.7% over the past month from above $4,700 levels.
stories.explain: Gold faces a dual headwind today: the Iran-Israel de-escalation removes the geopolitical risk premium, while strong jobs data pushes real interest rates higher as the nominal rate path shifts up with inflation expectations roughly stable. Gold has no yield, so higher real rates raise its opportunity cost — holding gold means forgoing a higher risk-free return. The month-long -9.7% decline from $4,700+ illustrates how quickly the geopolitical premium added during the Iran conflict has unwound; the 28.5% year-over-year gain reflects the structural buying from central banks and de-dollarization flows that provide a durable price floor even in risk-off unwinds.

stories.headline: SUMMER PORTAL ACTIVITY RESHAPES PROGRAMS — WASHINGTON LOSES THREE GUARDS
stories.body: Washington dropped three key guards — Zoom Diallo (15.7 ppg), JJ Mandaquit, and Courtland Muldrew — to the transfer portal, leaving the Huskies at eight scholarship players. Coach Danny Sprinkle added Texas Tech's LeJuan Watts and Gonzaga grad Steele Venters but needs five to six more additions before fall workouts.

stories.headline: WEMBANYAMA 32/8/6 SILENCES MSG, SPURS WIN GAME 3 — SERIES 2-1 KNICKS
stories.body: Victor Wembanyama posted 32 points, 8 rebounds, 6 assists, and 3 blocks as San Antonio won 115-111 at Madison Square Garden Monday, cutting New York's series lead to 2-1 and ending the Knicks' 13-game winning streak. Wembanyama shot 11-for-18, with 22 points coming at the rim or the free throw line. Game 4 is Wednesday June 10 at 8:30 PM ET on ABC.

stories.headline: 17 TEAMS OPEN MANDATORY MINICAMPS; SEAHAWKS BEGIN CHAMPIONSHIP DEFENSE
stories.body: Seattle opened mandatory minicamp Tuesday (June 9-11), signed OT Bobby Hart ahead of practice, and will hold their Super Bowl LX ring ceremony later this week. The Giants have Jaxson Dart and Jameis Winston both on the field adjusting to first-year coach John Harbaugh's offense. The regular season opens September 9 with a Super Bowl LX rematch.

stories.headline: INDIANA LANDS MICH. STATE WR NICK MARSH AS PROGRAMS FINALIZE SUMMER ROSTERS
stories.body: Indiana secured Michigan State wide receiver Nick Marsh — No. 3 WR and No. 12 overall in ESPN portal rankings — as programs make final roster moves before summer conditioning. Texas added No. 1 LB prospect Rasheem Biles. Washington's receiver corps remains thin after four portal exits this spring, though linebacker Isaiah Leilua committed to the Huskies.

deepDive.title: Why Good Jobs Data Tanks the Stock Market — The Rate Repricing Mechanism
content: Friday's May NFP print came in at 172,000 jobs — nearly double the 95,000 consensus — and the equity market's immediate reaction was to sell off sharply, with losses extending into Tuesday. That seems backward. A strong labor market signals a healthy economy, higher corporate revenues, and stronger earnings. Yet the S&P 500 is down 2.5% and the Nasdaq 100 down 3.4% over the past two sessions. Understanding why requires tracing the precise channel through which employment data affects equity prices.

The mechanism runs through discount rates. Every stock's theoretical price is the present value of its future cash flows: P = CF / (r − g), where r is the discount rate and g is growth. The discount rate is built from the risk-free rate plus an equity risk premium. When markets price in a Fed rate hike, the risk-free component of r rises by ~25 bps — and that flows through to every equity valuation simultaneously. The Nasdaq 100 fell harder than the S&P 500 because growth stocks are 'long duration': most of their value sits in cash flows 10-20 years out, and compounding a higher discount rate over a longer horizon produces disproportionately larger present value reductions. A 25 bps rate increase might cut a 2-year DCF by 0.3%, but a 20-year DCF by closer to 4%.

This dynamic is what traders call 'bad news is good news' (and vice versa). During 2022-2023, equity markets reliably rallied on weak payrolls because soft labor data reduced rate hike expectations — demonstrating the inverse relationship. The 2026 version is more dangerous: this labor strength comes alongside Iran-driven energy inflation, raising the specter of stagflation — the Fed forced to hike into a slowing growth environment. In a clean rate cycle, only 'r' moves in the DCF model. In stagflation, 'g' also deteriorates simultaneously, a double compression on valuations that the 1970s demonstrated could be prolonged. Goldman Sachs flagged this explicitly: a rate hike is not their base case, but the risk of a 'longer pause' is now live.

The immediate market setup: CME FedWatch prices a 68% probability of a December 2026 hike, up from 52% pre-NFP. If this week's May CPI release shows inflation still above 3% — likely given WTI averaged $90+ in May — hike probability may push above 80%, triggering another leg lower for growth stocks. The 10-year yield at 4.54% is still well below the 5.0%+ highs of late 2023; if data continues to surprise hot, a move toward 4.75-5.00% is live. Every 25 bps higher in the 10-year directly compresses the Shiller CAPE on a mechanical basis — and the NDX's heavy concentration in 30x+ forward earnings names means it remains the most exposed index if the rate repricing has further to run.
